items.title: Sangyadhi: An Analytical Framework for Diagnosing and Investigating Collective Care
items.abstract: While HCI has expanded from Personal to Family Informatics, researchers still lack a critical analytical vocabulary to diagnose what truly constitutes a collective care context. We introduce Sangyadhi, an analytical sociotechnical framework that synthesizes Situated Action, Distributed Cognition, the Capabilities Approach, and Actor-Network Theory to investigate multi-actor care ecologies. The framework articulates four interdependent analytical lenses: contextual grounding, distributed responsibility, trust-mediated sharing, and collaborative actionability. To demonstrate its diagnostic utility, we apply Sangyadhi to critically audit a decade of HCI digital health literature across self-tracking, family informatics, and clinical AI---surfacing structural omissions in how shifting authority, dynamic trust, and AI escalation are conceptualized. Ultimately, the goal of Sangyadhi is to equip researchers with an analytical blueprint for diagnosing observed care contexts, structuring field inquiries, and evaluating future technologies.

items.title: Saúde mental dos profissionais portuários: riscos psicossociais, prevenção e qualidade de vida no trabalho
items.abstract: Port work involves complex operations, productivity demands, exposure to occupational hazards and, in some roles, shifts and working hours that may contribute to physical and emotional strain. This article aims to analyze occupational and psychosocial factors related to the mental health of port workers and discuss prevention measures and the promotion of quality of working life. A qualitative, exploratory and descriptive bibliographic study was conducted, drawing on scientific articles, literature reviews, institutional documents and occupational health and safety regulations. The analysis identified relevant factors such as work overload, intense pace, noise, accident risks, irregular shifts, limited autonomy and insufficient social support. The literature indicates that prevention should integrate physical, ergonomic and psychosocial risks, with workers’ participation and organizational commitment. As an educational dissemination activity, the topic was also presented at EXPOTEC 2026 through an exhibition and interactive activities. This experience encouraged dialogue and the sharing of perceptions, but did not constitute field research or a systematic assessment of companies. The article concludes that protecting mental health in the port sector requires continuous risk management, communication, support and improvements in working conditions and work organization.

items.title: Scaling large language model-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication with human-in-the-loop evidence-calibrated selection
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the ability to scale clinical adjudication tasks traditionally dependent on exhaustive manual review. Line-of-therapy (LoT) adjudication, a major bottleneck in oncology cohort construction, is a prime example. Line boundaries must be inferred from longitudinal treatment histories according to nuanced, study-specific definitions, at every regimen transition for every patient. LLMs can apply this adjudication at scale, but their reliability varies across patients. Treatment histories differ in complexity, and ambiguous or atypical patterns depend on expert clinical judgment. Reliable automation thus requires verified support for model assignments and the ability to identify cases that warrant manual review. Here, we present evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework for scaling LLM-assisted LoT adjudication. ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and returns completed adjudications to the model as precedent. As the evidence base grows, ECS continuously calibrates confidence to estimate residual error, thus enabling more efficient use of clinician time. In simulations on 136 clinician adjudicated patients with multiple myeloma, ECS achieved a residual error of 5% after review of 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% when review was directed by LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling. These results support a scalable approach to study-specific LoT adjudication, using clinician evidence to inform automated predictions, minimize error, and reduce review burden.

items.title: Score-Based Stochastic Closure Modeling via Offline Indirect Learning and Online Data Assimilation
items.abstract: Stochastic closure modeling is an emerging area in reduced-order modeling of large and complex (e.g., multiscale, multi-physics) systems, for which the computationally affordable reduced-order physical descriptions (e.g., digital twins for additive manufacturing, world models for AI agents) in numerical simulations inevitably lead to information losses that cannot be well addressed by classical deterministic closures. However, learning stochastic closures typically requires closure data that are difficult to obtain from measurements or often prohibitively expensive to compute using first-principles simulations. In this work, we develop a stochastic closure modeling framework that builds on score-based diffusion models, leveraging indirect offline training and online data assimilation without requiring the direct data of closures. Numerical experiments on two-dimensional turbulent flows demonstrate that indirect offline learning captures key closure statistics and improves predictions of system state. In addition, combining the learned closure with known physical dynamics leads to better generalization capability across different regimes than purely data-driven models that directly predict system state. Compared to standard data assimilation methods with a Gaussian assumption, the posterior-score assimilation better represents non-Gaussian features of the learned closure, and its combination with state-level data assimilation further improves prediction of the system state. The proposed framework enables stochastic closure modeling in realistic and challenging scenarios of complex dynamical systems in mechanics and engineering problems, where non-Gaussian statistics of model-form uncertainties are non-negligible (e.g., due to the nonlinearities of the system dynamics and/or the observations) and true closure data are not available, for both offline learning and online assimilation.

items.title: SGIP: Learning Scene-Grounded Interaction Priors for Scene-Aware Human Motion Prediction
items.abstract: Human motion prediction (HMP) aims to forecast future movement from an observed motion sequence, and recent methods have incorporated 3D scene geometry and object semantics to improve long-term plausibility. However, the destination of future motion remains ambiguous in cluttered scenes: the same observed motion can lead to different interaction targets or navigation modes. Existing methods either handle this ambiguity implicitly or rely on auxiliary signals like gaze that are hard to obtain in practice. To address this, we propose SGIP, which explicitly predicts where in the scene future motion will be grounded across both objects and open navigation regions, and uses it to condition future trajectory and full-body pose prediction. This scene-grounded interaction prior is learned via intent distillation: at training time only, a teacher model scores candidate scene regions by combining an LLM prompted with a textual description of the person's intent with geometric motion-scene features. A student model learns to reproduce these scores from only the observed motion and 3D scene, making intent and LLM unnecessary at test time. Across multiple benchmark datasets, SGIP outperforms prior scene-aware baselines on both trajectory and pose accuracy in a realistic deployment setting where neither gaze nor intent is available at inference, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The project page is available at https://sgip2026.github.io.

items.title: Socrates went nuclear: Comparing Interaction Strategies for AI systems in a Learning Context using Brain Sensing
items.abstract: Students are adopting LLMs at scale. This poses a question: does unrestricted AI access bypass the cognitive effort required for learning, or does it streamline knowledge acquisition? This paper reports on a study where we compare three designs for user-AI interaction in a learning context: (1) an unrestricted conversational bot like ChatGPT, (2) a pedagogically constrained bot that guides through hints without giving final answers, which we refer to as the Socratic mode; and (3) a non-conversational adaptive tutoring system that adjusts difficulty in real-time based on the user’s cognitive engagement derived from the brain signals. Fifty study participants were tasked with learning about nuclear safety protocols, a domain chosen for its zero-prior knowledge baseline. The participants progressed through an instructional video, a pre-test, an AI-driven assessment phase, which varied in the three conditions, and an immediate post-test. The nature of the questions centered primarily on factual knowledge acquisition, but it still required participants to have a global understanding of the concepts in order to answer the questions correctly. A Muse headband was used to derive the cognitive engagement of all users in all conditions. The unrestricted chatbot produced higher learning gains (delta) than both constrained modes ( p <.03, d > 0.80), while the adaptive condition generated significantly higher EEG engagement ( p =.018). The cluster analysis of chatbot usage and discussion patterns by users showed that most participants in the unrestricted-mode adopted a direct answer-retrieval strategy, while participants in the Socratic-mode initially attempted to reason through the hints before progressively disengaging. Consequently, this also suggests that the success of the unrestricted AI is not an evidence of deeper learning, but rather a result of the immediate post-test evaluation after the training phase.

items.title: Take a Step Back: A Dual-Granularity Raw Feature Empowered Intermediate Fusion Graph Convolutional Network for Multimodal Recommendation
items.abstract: Although multimodal recommendations have shown the ability to learn user preferences and item properties by leveraging explicit multimodal information, they remain constrained by two critical limitations: low-quality representation learning and modality fusion. For the former, existing solutions primarily focus on multi-granularity representation learning; however, we argue that training such representations is difficult due to the inherent data sparsity problem in recommendation scenarios. For the latter, existing solutions often rely on contrastive learning to align representations of different modalities to facilitate modality fusion, yet alignment-only objectives may over-compress valuable modality-specific information. To this end, we suggest \underline{``Take a Step Back"} and propose a \textbf{D}ual-granularity raw feature empowered \textbf{I}ntermediate fusion \textbf{G}raph \textbf{C}onvolutional \textbf{N}etwork (\textbf{DIGCN}) for multimodal recommendation. DIGCN leverages the multimodal understanding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct dual-granularity raw features directly. Furthermore, DIGCN introduces an intermediate fusion graph convolutional network equipped with dynamic cross-modality weight correction, designed to capture cross-modality signals and achieve effective modality fusion. Comprehensive experiments on four real-world datasets validate that DIGCN consistently outperforms a variety of strong baselines. Additional analyses confirm its superiority under varying levels of data sparsity and cold-start scenarios. Notably, DIGCN demonstrates high extensibility, capable of further benefiting from additional contrastive learning-based alignment tasks.

items.title: Technical competence, occupational health and safety, and environment predict contractor employee performance
items.abstract: Applied studies of employee performance in Indonesian technical firms usually ask which factor dominates. This study asks instead whether technical competence, occupational health and safety (OHS), and the work environment behave as rival levers or as a bundle of resources. A census survey of all 41 employees of PT Multi Jaya Teknik, an electrical and mechanical contractor in Batu Bara Regency, North Sumatra, measured each construct with a five-item Likert scale (α = .807-.903), and performance was regressed on the three predictors by ordinary least squares. The predictors jointly explained a large share of variance, R² = .602 (adjusted R² = .570), F(3, 37) = 18.65, p < .001. Technical competence (B = 0.372, 95% CI [0.035, 0.709], f² = 0.135), OHS (B = 0.290, 95% CI [0.048, 0.532], f² = 0.159), and work environment (B = 0.261, 95% CI [0.018, 0.504], f² = 0.127) each retained a unique positive association, with closely matched standardized weights (β = .267-.335) and overlapping intervals. Because the smallest individual effect the design could detect was f² = 0.202, each estimate is individually fragile, whereas the joint effect is clear. The pattern is interpreted as safe competence: in hazardous field work, capability, safety provision, and workable conditions act as non-redundant resources, so no single lever should be expected to dominate. The study also shows that perceived OHS provision predicts self-rated performance, not accident prevention, and it offers a complete reporting template for small single-firm samples.

items.title: The Impact of Situational Awareness on Organisational Resilience and Performance in Healthcare Organisations: An Integrative Review
items.abstract: Hospitals and health systems are complex adaptive systems. Safe care, continuity of services and the ability to adapt under pressure all depend on people noticing what is happening, making sense of it and anticipating what comes next. Situational awareness (SA), a concept that grew out of military aviation and human factors engineering, is now built into clinical non-technical skills frameworks, organisational resilience models and crisis management practice.

items.title: THE ROLE OF HEALTH LITERACY IN PREVENTING OCCUPATIONAL DISEASES AMONG MINERS
items.abstract: This article examines the role of health literacy in preventing occupational diseases among miners in Uzbekistan. It focuses on miners’ ability to understand workplace health information, apply it during routine tasks, and communicate concerns to supervisors and occupational health professionals. Using exposure to respirable dust and excessive noise as examples, the article considers how miners can interpret the purpose of exposure controls, report problems with protective measures, and understand the role of periodic health examinations. It also examines how plain-language instructions, practical demonstrations, and asking workers to explain procedures in their own words can help occupational health teams identify misunderstandings during training. Health literacy is considered alongside engineering controls, exposure monitoring, and health surveillance within a workplace prevention programme. For medical students, the article illustrates how occupational health consultations can connect a miner’s work history with the hazards encountered on the job and communicate preventive measures in terms relevant to the worker’s daily tasks.

items.title: The Scientific Approach as an Accelerator of Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Healthcare: The LifeLink Monitoring Mode
items.abstract: This article asks how a scientific, evidence-generating approach can speed up the adoption of artificial intelligence in healthcare. We use LifeLink Monitoring as an applied case and combine a structured literature review, market and regulatory analysis, competitive benchmarking, stakeholder surveys and expert interviews, scenario modelling, and pilot design. The analysis reveals a persistent shortage of context-specific evidence on clinical utility, workflow integration, human factors, economics, and governance. To address it, we propose an Evidence-to-Adoption Framework in which staged pilots turn technological hypotheses into evidence that clinicians, managers, regulators, payers, and investors can act on. We treat acceleration as a proposed mechanism that requires prospective testing, not as a demonstrated outcome, and we specify how it can be measured.

items.title: Towards a foundation model for Type IIB flux vacua
items.abstract: Progress in characterising the Type IIB flux landscape requires scalable methods for constructing flux vacua. In this work, we investigate generative models as a framework for sampling vacua across multiple Calabi-Yau geometries and for directing searches towards specified physical properties. We compare transformers and diffusion models trained to generate quantised fluxes together with approximate values of the complex structure moduli and axio-dilaton. We exploit a staged training procedure comprising pre-training, and post-training via reinforcement learning, and assess how each stage improves the generated distributions and enables targeted sampling. We further examine whether structures learned from geometries with smaller $h^{1,2}$ can be transferred to geometries with larger $h^{1,2}$ through fine-tuning on specialised datasets. Our results provide evidence that generative models can learn distributions of flux vacua across distinct compactifications, improve searches for vacua with selected properties and transfer information between geometries. This establishes a concrete basis for developing a foundation model of the Type IIB flux landscape.

items.title: Towards Agentic Scientific Discovery in Distributed Systems
items.abstract: We investigate when adaptive tool selection helps identify a shared equation across clients with different input coverage. Query-ATLAS (query-conditioned Agentic Tool-based Learning for Aggregating Symbolic Equations) uses an LLM to guide symbolic search from client errors and previous proposals in a simulated distributed system. A four-architecture comparison reveals task-dependent opportunities: relative to fixed PySR-LLM, validation acceptances rise from 3/12 to 7/12 on CRK3 and from 11/12 to 12/12 on oscillator2, while MatSci3 favors the fixed workflow. Across 72 settings in a post-hoc six-task subset of eight development tasks, Query-ATLAS achieves 64 validation and 64 in-distribution passes, versus 62 and 59 for the fixed workflow; both pass 47/60 eligible out-of-distribution tests. The fixed workflow retains lower median errors and cost. Broader query coverage emerges as a promising benefit, motivating task-aware tool selection and client-aware fitting for scientific agents.

items.title: Translating Multi-Agent Traffic Logic into On-Demand Human-Vehicle Dialogue
items.abstract: Unsignalized roundabouts remain challenging for connected and autonomous vehicles because of dynamic merges, spatial conflicts, and communication constraints. We present a decentralized coordination architecture based on Group Mutual Exclusion (GME), in which each conflict point is treated as a local critical section and compatible virtual platoons may be admitted concurrently. A lead vehicle aggregates requests from its physical queue and relays admission decisions to following vehicles. To make this safety-critical process intelligible to occupants, we introduce a query-driven small language model (SLM) interface that reads structured controller traces and produces explanations only when requested. The SLM is strictly read-only and cannot alter GME decisions. We illustrate how traces containing conflict, priority, and waiting-time information can support contextual explanations of yielding, deceleration, and merging. The work provides an architecture and feasibility demonstration. Quantitative traffic, language-model, and human-factors evaluations are left to future work.

items.title: TRANSLATING POWER: AI, MEDIATION AND THE IMAGINARY OF MANIPULATION IN ACADEMIC CONTEXTS
items.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence in academic writing and translation is changing not only the speed of textual production but also the ways in which linguistic authority is constructed and perceived. In multilingual academic contexts, AI systems translate, reformulate, and refine texts according to dominant conventions of academic English. Such assistance may widen access to international communication, yet its fluency can also make the interpretative choices embedded in the resulting text less visible. This article examines AI-mediated Romanian-English academic translation as a site where linguistic assistance, symbolic power, and the imaginary of manipulation intersect. The study approaches translation as mediation rather than neutral transfer. It asks how AI may reshape lexical authority, epistemic stance, and stylistic identity, how these changes influence the perceived legitimacy of academic discourse, and when unobtrusive mediation may acquire a potentially manipulative effect. The theoretical discussion connects translation studies with scholarship on symbolic power, academic stance, and sociotechnical imaginaries. Methodologically, the article adopts a conceptual qualitative approach supported by three illustrative Romanian-English micro-analyses. These examples are not treated as a representative corpus and do not support statistical generalisation. Instead, they reveal how apparently minor lexical, epistemic, and stylistic reformulations can influence authority, certainty, and authorial visibility. The article argues that manipulation should not be equated automatically with factual distortion or deliberate ideological intent. It may also arise through naturalisation, when a fluent and plausible formulation is accepted as transparent or inevitable. The article concludes that responsible AI-assisted academic translation requires comparison with the source, attention to shifts in certainty, agency and rhetorical positioning, and clear human responsibility for the final text. For translators, writers and educators, critical AI literacy entails treating generated language as a proposal to be evaluated rather than as an impersonal solution.

items.title: Turning Errors into Successes: Designing LLM Tutoring Around Scaffolded Error Correction
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) could make personalized tutoring available at scale, but it remains unclear how they can best support the instructional processes that make one-on-one instruction effective. We compared two ways of using LLMs after students make errors: providing personalized explanations of those errors, or engaging students in additional cycles of scaffolded practice and feedback, with a Socratic tutor guiding students toward the correct answer. In a preregistered online experiment, 400 adults practiced setting up constraint equations and, after each attempt, received the correct answer, a generic explanation, a personalized LLM explanation of their error, or Socratic tutoring. Socratic tutoring helped: participants resolved 64% of their errors through the dialogue and scored 0.24 SD higher on practice-aligned posttest questions than those who received generic or personalized explanations. Socratic participants also found the session more interesting, less frustrating, and less costly, even though it took nearly twice as long. In contrast, we found no evidence of a benefit of personalized explanations over generic ones, and neither type of explanation reliably outperformed simply seeing the correct answer. These findings suggest that LLM tutors may add the most value not by explaining errors more precisely but by helping students correct those errors themselves through scaffolded practice. This pattern fits a mastery-experience account of tutoring, in which an effective tutor notices when a student is struggling, steps in with guidance, and works with the student until the struggle resolves into success. AI tutors may be most effective when designed around this principle.

items.title: Understanding Users' Security, Privacy, and Trust Concerns in Healthcare AI Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into healthcare systems, from clinical information retrieval to workflow automation and decision support, which introduces new security, privacy, and trust risks with direct implications for patient care. While prior work has examined these risks from technical and regulatory perspectives, less is known about how these risks are naturally discussed in online communities. To address this gap, we conduct a large-scale analysis of 14 medical communities on Reddit and extract 6,514 relevant posts. Through systematic qualitative coding and LLM-assisted classification, we investigate concerns expressed in healthcare AI discussions, their prevalence, and how they evolve over time. Our analysis reveals that users perceive healthcare AI as expanding traditional healthcare trust boundaries and attack surfaces through integrations with electronic health records, third-party services, cloud platforms, and automated clinical workflows. Posts express concerns about over-privileged access to sensitive records, opaque data flows, unauthorized secondary use, and unsafe automation can amplify the consequences of errors and misuse. We identify four attitudes toward these risks: exploring questions of accountability and harm, cautiously accepting AI with stronger safeguards, skepticism about system trustworthiness, and resignation to growing data exposure and automation. Longitudinal analysis shows that SP&T discussions have increased significantly, with shifts coinciding with major healthcare AI deployments, privacy incidents, and regulatory developments. These findings illuminate changing trust relationships and data-governance challenges, informing the design and governance of safer, more transparent, and accountable healthcare AI systems.

items.title: Vibe Interventions: Can Users Personalize and Iterate Their Way to Behavior Change?
items.abstract: Recent advances in large language models allow a working application to be generated from natural-language description, and is referred to as generative user interfaces. Their application to behavior change is unexplored, and we provide one of the first controlled investigations of it. We distinguish two components of authorship: iteration, the revision of a generated artifact in natural language, and personalization, the conditioning of generation on stated context. In a pre-registered between-subjects experiment (N = 300, 60 per condition), we crossed these two factors and added a static intervention as a control, yielding five conditions; participants stated a goal and received a generated intervention. The personalized generative condition ranked highest on every self-report outcome, including ownership, satisfaction, and intended adoption. Randomized iteration had no detectable effect, and higher revision counts were negatively associated with evaluative ratings. This work establishes which component of authorship carries motivational value in generative behavior change tools.

items.title: VoiceGuard: An Audio-Native LLM-VLA Pipeline for Wheelchair-Mounted Assistive Manipulation
items.abstract: Wheelchair-mounted robotic arms can help people with limited upper-limb mobility reach and manipulate everyday objects, but operating them typically requires stepwise joystick control and frequent mode switching. Natural-language interfaces could let users express task-level goals, yet they must handle ambiguous requests, distinguish commands from nearby conversation, and support interruption. We present VoiceGuard, a voice interface that separates spoken intent from robot execution through structured request validation and a local stop mechanism. On-device detectors handle the wake phrase and stop commands, an audio-native large language model (LLM) routes each request into a structured function packet, a rule-based ToolDispatcher accepts, rejects, or clarifies the packet, and a SmolVLA vision-language-action (VLA) policy executes accepted tasks on a low-cost SO-101 arm. Preliminary tests showed that the system correctly handled 55 of 60 voice commands, including ambiguous and non-directed utterances, completed 16 of 20 deliveries, and stopped the arm on all 20 stop commands with a median latency of 210 ms. We demonstrate the feasibility of combining flexible spoken input with constrained task execution and local interruption for wheelchair-mounted assistive manipulation.

items.title: Watching Yourself or an Expert? Effects of Avatar Motion Source During Outdoor Jogging
items.abstract: Outdoor jogging provides limited opportunities for runners to observe and improve their movement in real time. We developed a wearable jogging support system that presents either the runner’s own movement or expert movement using an avatar. A within-subjects study with 13 recreational joggers found no significant differences in intrinsic motivation, flow, or objective running performance. However, participants perceived the two motion sources differently: the expert-motion avatar was perceived as more capable and tended to evoke a stronger sense of running together, whereas participants more frequently reported using the self-motion avatar to inspect their own running form. Interestingly, only half of the participants recognized the expert-motion avatar as representing highly skilled running, highlighting that the effectiveness of avatar-based feedback depends not only on presenting expert movement but also on whether users recognize it as expert-level.

items.title: Where Should LLM Agents Adapt at Test Time? In Context, in Weights, or Both
items.abstract: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. items.title: Where the Savings Go: The Limits of Hiding Cross-Tenant Cache Hits in LLM Serving
items.abstract: LLM serving engines cache prompt prefixes; a cache hit skips computation and returns faster, so a shared cache reveals whether others have sent a given text. Per-account salting closes this channel but forgoes cross-tenant reuse and isolates only whole accounts, even where access is redistributed or trust domains are subdivided below them. Defenses that share globally but hide hits promise reuse without relying on account boundaries. Hiding a hit requires everything tenants observe afterwards to be distributed as if it had missed. The defenses we examine target the hit-miss gap; we instead follow where the saved time goes. Step-based schedulers that never idle while work waits pass it in full to every request queued behind the hit, shifting each earlier by the same amount. An attacker within ordinary rate limits brackets a probe with two groups of listeners that each return one token, sends them in one short burst, and counts in how many steps they finish. Replaying a production trace on one vLLM instance at up to half capacity, a single probe detects cached texts of 256 tokens or more with advantage at least 0.98. Hiding only the hit request falls to one probe on vLLM and SGLang; random delays must reach about ten times the shift or more to cut the advantage to 0.1; narrowing what is shared gives no guarantee against this inference. Since any observable tenant benefit is also a signal, we prove that a rate-limited tenant's gain from content written by k other accounts is at most of order k times the leakage allowed, whatever the provider does with identities; at zero leakage, only the provider keeps the savings. Exact hiding is attainable in principle on one instance, but mechanisms that only pause or hold work know skipped work's duration only approximately, so under saturated prefill they must pad every step that may hold a hit, at a price that grows with time rather than with hits.

items.title: Work-Related Health Hazards, Preventive Practices, and Their Predictors among Secondary School Teachers in Ilorin South Local Government Area, Kwara State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Introduction: Teachers are exposed to physical, ergonomic, psychosocial and biological hazards at work. This study assessed the prevalence of work-related health hazards, preventive practices and perceived predictors of preventive practice among secondary school teachers in Ilorin South Local Government Area (LGA), Kwara State, Nigeria. Methodology: A descriptive cross-sectional survey of 362 public and private secondary school teachers used multistage sampling and a structured, self-administered four-point Likert questionnaire. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, proportions with 95% confidence intervals, Pearson correlation and binary logistic regression (α = 0.05). Results: Exposure was highest for heavy workload and large classes and lowest for biological hazards (65.5%); all exceeded 50%. Preventive practice was inconsistent (grand mean = 2.49), with hand hygiene highest (2.77) and protective equipment use lowest (2.14). Exposure correlated weakly with practice (r = .237, p < .001). In the logistic model (Nagelkerke R² = .255), institutional support (OR = 2.20) and belief in prevention (OR = 1.86) predicted adoption, and perceived socio-demographic influence was negatively associated (OR = 0.75). Conclusion: Hazard exposure is high and practice uneven. Institutional support and belief in effectiveness were the strongest predictors. Schools should strengthen occupational health support, and health education should address beliefs about prevention.

items.title: XAI as a Trust Calibration Mechanism in Teleoperated Human-Agent Systems: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: As teleoperated systems increasingly incorporate autonomous agents capable of independent decision-making, the human operator transitions from a direct controller to a delegated supervisor. This shift introduces a fundamental challenge: how operators calibrate their trust toward agents whose decisions they cannot interpret. Miscalibrated trust, whether overtrust leading to unsafe delegation or undertrust causing inefficient over-intervention, represents one of the most consequential human factors risks in agentic teleoperation. This paper argues that Explainable AI (XAI) mechanisms constitute a promising but underexplored lever for dynamic trust calibration in teleoperated human-agent systems. A three-layer conceptual framework is proposed that maps operator profiles to adaptive XAI modality selection and closes the loop through a trust feedback mechanism that dynamically adjusts the agent’s level of autonomy. Three application scenarios, namely robotic surgical assistance, hazardous environment inspection, and remote industrial maintenance, are examined to illustrate how the framework operates under realistic teleoperation constraints. The paper identifies key research challenges and outlines a forward-looking agenda for empirically grounding the proposed framework.

items.title: 'We just went with what seemed the best supported': Lessons on Cryptographic Practices in Securing Microcontrollers from Embedded CTFs
items.abstract: Microcontroller-based embedded systems support safety- and security-critical applications yet provide insufficient resources for modern cryptography. While numerous lightweight primitives and libraries have been proposed, little is known about how practitioners select and deploy them. We bridge this gap with a mixed-methods study of the 2023 and 2024 MITRE Embedded Capture-the-Flag (eCTF) competitions. We review 47 working firmware submissions and hold 22 semi-structured interviews with team members. Our analysis reveals two classes of findings. 1) General lessons echo broader usability and human-factors challenges observed in other domains: Developers favor speed and integration convenience over stronger security guarantees, and unclear documentation poses greater barriers to implementing cryptographic functionality than raw resource limits. 2) Embedded-specific lessons highlight unique challenges in resource-constrained environments: Side-channel hardening receives disproportionate attention compared to protecting data at rest, platform heterogeneity complicates portable privacy-preserving implementations, and limited debugging and verification support make it difficult to validate security properties at runtime. We group these findings into implementation practices, participant insights, and practical challenges while giving concrete advice for researchers, educators, device vendors, and the open-source community. Our results show how cryptography is applied in today's security-oriented embedded projects and outline near-term steps to make these systems safer and easier to build.

items.title: "It Scams In The Family:" GenAI Voice Cloning Scams among Sighted and Families with Blind or Low Vision Members
items.abstract: The usual victim in phone scams is an individual at risk of being defrauded or whose identity might be stolen. But a new scamming scheme has emerged, targeting families as victims instead - an individual at risk of being defrauded through an emergency request, voiced by a clone of a related individual whose voice identity has been non-consensually sampled. As these scams are harmful both to the well-being and individuals' true identity (voice), in addition to financial loss, we set to ''conceptually replicate'' an early exploration done by Sharevski et al. (2025) through naturalistically resembling experiences with n1=10 families involving sighted and n2=10 involving a blind or a low vision member (pairs of a 'caller' and 'callee', n=40 total). Our thematic analysis uncovered an overarching attitude of ''self-preparedness'' to withstand these scams, based on both 'intrinsic' motivation to ward off pressure to act on an emotional impulse and 'extrinsic' motivation to avoid immediate and long-term victimization. Expanding the original study's findings with the experiences of a population reliant on voice both as a medium and as an access, we draw on the resilience themes to sketch out 'user-sensitive' accessible designs against GenAI scams.

items.title: “When AI Can Do the Task, Is Learning Still Worth It and Am I Capable?” Scales for Learning Value and Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI and Links to AI Use and Academic Outcomes
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now perform many academic tasks that students were once required to master, raising the question of whether learners still value learning for themselves and feel capable of learning without relying on AI. Available scales mainly focus on AI as the outcome of learning rather than the context of it. This study developed and validated brief scales measuring Learning Value in the Context of AI (LV-AI, the value of personally learning when associated tasks can be performed by AI) and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI (LSE-AI, the appraisal of ability to learn and perform academically without relying on AI) and examined their associations with AI use and academic outcomes (effort expenditure, persistence, GPA). Data were collected from 882 undergraduate students in the U.S. with approximately equal traditional-age and adult learners. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis supported a correlated two-factor structure. Both scales showed acceptable reliability (ω = .81 and .72), discriminant validity from classical task value and self-efficacy, and measurement invariance across student age type. When classical task value, classical self-efficacy, and AI use were controlled, LV-AI and LSE-AI incrementally predicted effort and persistence, but not GPA. Moreover, although AI use showed a significant negative association with academic effort, an exploratory mediation analysis indicated that this association no longer held when learners' LV-AI and LSE-AI were accounted for, with the indirect path carrying over half of the initial association. This highlights the important role these AI-embedded constructs play in preventing the disengagement tendencies.

items.title: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability
items.abstract: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.

items.title: A Spatiotemporal Collision Avoidance Support System for Remote Operators of MASSs
items.abstract: Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASSs) require timely human intervention when collision risks develop. This study presents a spatiotemporal decision-support framework that maps Velocity Obstacle (VO) collision-risk directions onto ownship-centered time rings using target-specific times to closest point of approach. The resulting Areas of Reachable Collision (ARCs) are used to generate course-alteration plans and visualize spatiotemporal risks. ARCs and original VO were compared in AIS-based simulations and, under matched nominal prediction horizons, in a 30 min training scenario. ARC generated avoidance plans, but prescribed passing clearances were not consistently maintained in the matched-horizon scenario, and route-rejoining outcomes varied across settings. Implementation in a remote-operation simulator was accompanied by an exploratory analysis of 26 training records. The study demonstrates technical feasibility but does not establish improved operator understanding or causal human-performance benefits.

items.title: A subspecialty diagnostic system powered by self-supervised learning for cervical histopathology
items.abstract: Cervical cancer remains a major malignancy in women, with large-scale human papillomavirus-based screening generating a large volume of biopsies and, for advanced cases, surgical specimens, imposing an overwhelming diagnostic burden that necessitates precise histopathological evaluation. Although deep learning shows promise, general foundation models offer a broader reach but remain limited in capturing subspecialty-specific features and task adaptability. We introduce the Cervical Subspecialty Pathology (CerS-Path) diagnostic system, built upon the subspecialized dataset and developed through two synergistic pretraining stages: self-supervised learning on approximately 190 million tissue patches to build a cervical-specific feature extractor, and multimodal enhancement with 2.5 million image-text pairs, followed by diagnostic functions integration and downstream task enhancement. CerS-Path integrates eight functions—across morphological diagnosis, predictive analytics, and multimodal tasks—to cover the diagnostic workflow from biopsies to resection specimens. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate improved performance in cervical pathology in female patients, where CerS-Path outperforms state-of-the-art foundation models across 26 of 30 diagnostic tasks. Furthermore, in multicenter retrospective and prospective validation across six independent cohorts of women, CerS-Path achieves up to 99% sensitivity for clinically relevant lesion detection with acceptable specificity across sites, highlighting its potential for screening-derived histopathology and suitability for integration into high-volume diagnostic pathways. Foundation models could be promising for cervical cancer screening, but have important limitations for their clinical deployment. Here, the authors introduce the Cervical Subspecialty Pathology (CerS-Path) diagnostic system, a self-supervised learning framework for cervical cancer pathology that outperforms state-of-the-art foundation models across multiple diagnostic tasks.

items.title: Adaptive Occupational Health and Safety Management in Coastal Revetment Construction: A Case Study of the Candidasa Beach Conservation Project, Bali.
items.abstract: Coastal revetment construction in tourism areas involves dynamic occupational health and safety risks due to direct exposure to tides, waves, currents, extreme weather, and public activities. This study examines adaptive Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) management in the Candidasa Beach Conservation Project, Bali. A qualitative descriptive case study was conducted using project documents, including the Construction Safety Plan, Job Safety Analysis–Construction Safety Analysis, daily OHS reports, RKL–RPL documents, and technical-environmental reports. The analysis focused on the relationship between oceanographic dynamics, safety risks, and adaptive control measures. The findings show that oceanographic conditions are key triggers of fluctuating safety risks affecting workers, equipment, and the public. Adaptive OHS management is reflected in safety planning, work-method adjustment, tidal-based scheduling, marine-specific personal protective equipment, and public access control. The study highlights the need for contextual and responsive OHS systems in coastal construction projects.

items.title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
items.abstract: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by \(17.6\%\) (WS-21) and \(17.0\%\) (Mean-L1), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from 3.1 × to 2.3 ×. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50 M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48 B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population–rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.

items.title: AEGIS-AIR v2.0 — Aircraft Safety Monitoring and Early-Warning Framework
items.abstract: AEGIS-AIR v2.0 — Research Description AEGIS-AIR is a proposed aircraft safety monitoring and early-warning framework designed to support the detection, assessment, and prioritization of potential in-flight hazards. The conceptual architecture integrates distributed sensing across aircraft structural, propulsion, hydraulic, electrical, thermal, and environmental systems. It explores sensor-data fusion, anomaly scoring, weighted risk assessment, critical-alert logic, probabilistic reliability analysis, and estimates of time remaining before predefined safety thresholds may be reached. The framework also considers the integration of certified weather-monitoring information and the assessment of uncertain airborne hazards, subject to sensor limitations, operational constraints, and aviation safety requirements. The accompanying mathematical appendix presents illustrative analytical formulations, while the technical infographics describe the proposed system architecture and monitoring workflow. This document presents a theoretical research proposal. The framework has not been experimentally validated, flight-tested, certified, or demonstrated to improve aircraft safety. Further simulation, engineering verification, human-factors assessment, and regulatory evaluation would be required before any operational application.

items.title: Agent Authenticator: Passkey-Grade, Hardware-Bound Authentication for AI Agents
items.abstract: AI coding agents now push code, publish packages, call model APIs and operate cloud resources on behalf of developers. They authenticate to these services with the same bearer secrets humans use, personal access tokens, API keys and package-registry tokens, stored where the model, its subprocesses and any co-resident malware can read them. Incidents in 2025 and 2026, including prompt-injection attacks on coding agents and self-propagating supply-chain worms, show that this arrangement fails in predictable ways. Passkeys solved the analogous problem for humans, but they require a human gesture on every use and cannot be operated by an autonomous process. We present the Agent Authenticator, a design that gives agents passkey-grade authentication properties: per-service hardware-bound keys, no shared secrets, origin binding enforced by the runtime rather than the model, normalized attestation of the execution environment, human-signed scoped mandates, and cross-device human approval for high-risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on developer laptops and in cloud enclaves, and it deploys as a profile over existing mechanisms, MCP authorization, OAuth token exchange including the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, git and SSH, rather than as a new identity system. The authenticator also produces a signed, hash-chained record of each action it authorizes. We analyze the design against a threat model centered on prompt injection and same-host compromise, map it onto five documented incidents, and discuss its limits.

items.title: AI Inference-Aware Optimal Power Flow: Converting Token Requirements into Grid Flexibility
items.abstract: The rapid growth, temporal variability, and geographic concentration of electricity demand from artificial intelligence (AI) inference can aggravate transmission congestion near data centers (DCs). The spatial and temporal flexibility of inference workloads offers an opportunity to alleviate this congestion: requests can be routed across DCs or deferred within users' quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. However, inference routing primarily considers graphics processing unit (GPU) availability, leaving this flexibility underused in grid operation. Using GPU measurements, this paper models inference latency and DC power consumption to quantify the flexibility available under users' time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL) requirements. These models are then incorporated into an AI inference-aware optimal power flow (OPF) that coordinates inference routing and power system operation among DC operators, the transmission system operator, and inference users. By linking user requests, token generation at DCs, and electricity delivery through the transmission network, the formulation schedules inference workloads subject to both users' QoS requirements and transmission constraints. Simulations on the PJM system show that, compared with computing-based routing and with electricity price-based routing, coordinating inference routing with network operation enables growing DC electricity demand deliverable to be met at lower cost.

items.title: An Integrated Epistemic–Algorithmic Architecture for Conflicting Data: Grading Witnesses, Counting Origins, and Measuring Certainty
items.abstract: This project turns methods from classical Islamic scholarship into an engineering method for deciding what to believe when data sources disagree, and tests the parts it can with pre-registered experiments. Every registered result is published, including the failures. Where each part comes from, and where it is measured: - Hadith criticism (al-jarh wa-l-ta'dil): grading witnesses. - Each source is graded on a training split with known answers, and scored on a separate test split. - Sources that repeat the same errors are counted once (makhraj). - Weak-but-honest sources are strengthened only by independent routes (al-hasan li-ghayrih, after Ibn al-Salah's Muqaddima). - A source is checked against reliable peers (i'tibar; designed, found infeasible, not tested). - The documented method of Sheikh Abu Ishaq al-Huwayni guides the reviews. - Al-Khwarizmi: balance and restoration (al-jabr wa-l-muqabala). Every algorithm states invariants (renaming, copying, permuting labels), and these become metamorphic tests and mutation tests of the analysis code itself. The share of planted faults caught is reported, not assumed. - Al-Ghazali: degrees of certainty. Every claim is labelled by what supports it: reasoning, measurement, or independent replication. None has yet been independently replicated. Causal claims require an intervention, not a correlation. - Ibn al-Haytham: the critic as adversary. From the crowd study on, an AI agent configured as a statistical referee reviewed each protocol before it ran, and the hasan protocol also had an AI red-team review; Flight and Stock had neither. No independent human referee has reviewed any protocol. - Maqasid: purpose and harm. Each deliverable is reviewed for benefit and harm, with a named human responsible. Studies, in order: 1. Flight. Committed to version control (git only, not a third-party registry) before running. The method scored 97.56% [seed range 96.70–98.05] against 95.00% [93.72–96.15] for our simplified AccuCopy, reimplemented from its paper. The brackets are ranges over five splits of one dataset, not confidence intervals, and no interval was computed for the difference. Removing copy detection cost 1.57 points (a mean over seeds, no interval). 2. Stock, https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/CKNDG. Five registered hypotheses passed. H2 compared precision at partial coverage with accuracy at full coverage, an unlike comparison, and is not cited as evidence. Post hoc, the reference (nasdaq.com) was also one of the sources. Without it, the method scored 90.63% [split range 89.93–91.44, not a confidence interval] against 79.56% for a simplified per-attribute weighted vote built after the results, with no interval for the difference; makhraj's contribution fell from +1.73 to −0.24 points; and coverage with abstention fell to 89.10%, below H2's 90%. 3. Crowdsourced labels, https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QK72X. The general claim was withdrawn: Dawid–Skene won. No copying groups were detected, which does not prove the workers independent. 4. Hasan li-ghayrih on Web relevance labels, https://osf.io/fhuxz. Withdrawn. H1 (hasan against the registered isnad) passed, +5.67 points [95% cluster-bootstrap CI 4.62, 6.77]. H2 (hasan against the strongest Dawid–Skene) failed, −2.32 [−3.71, −0.94]. H4 (weak workers' true weight against zero weight) failed, −2.84 [−3.64, −2.03]: zeroing the weak workers was better. 5. Isnad over LLM ensembles. Not run; in preparation. A post hoc reading, not a tested hypothesis: - The method led on two web datasets with copying (on Stock partly because the reference was itself a source). - It led on none of the three crowd datasets whose registered run completed (product, sentiment, relevance); on game the registered run crashed. A post hoc lead on game (94.59 against 94.17) reversed to −0.18 under a 30-second answer window and was withdrawn as evidence. The registered isnad also lost on Web relevance (80.67 against 88.65). Which property explains this is untested. Prior work is credited in each study. AI assistance: The research question and its ideas are the author's. He directed the work, approved everything published, and is responsible for it. Code, analysis, drafting and much of the protocol and method design were carried out with AI agents (Claude) under his direction, and every review so far, including these corrections, is by AI agents.

items.title: Analysis of patent data and criteria for patentability in furniture design: focus on the CPC/IPC A47D classification for children’s furniture
items.abstract: In the furniture industry, the originality of products and their competitiveness in the market are directly linked to the proper management of intellectual property rights. Children’s furniture, in particular, lies at the intersection of aesthetic design and technical innovation because it must meet functional requirements such as safety, modularity, ergonomics, and convertibility. This study examines the patentability criteria for children’s furniture (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability) and highlights the legal and technical distinctions between design registration and patents/utility models. Additionally, it addresses the methodology of prior art searches (patent searches) to prevent redundant investments in R&D and design processes. Within the scope of this study, the main class A47D and its subclasses corresponding to children’s furniture under the International Patent Classification (IPC/CPC), as well as the Locarno Classification (Class 06) used for industrial designs, are detailed, and effective search strategies and query combinations in databases are presented. The findings of this research are intended to provide insights for future researchers regarding the patenting of furniture designs, patentability criteria, and the R&D and design processes for children’s furniture.

items.title: Application of Design Thinking to Develop an Ergonomic Auxiliary for Heavy Mold Handling in Injection Molding Operations
items.abstract: Manual handling of heavy molds in plastic injection molding operations constitutes a significant source of physical effort, fatigue, and musculoskeletal risk for machine operators. Molds typically weighing between 15 and 30 kg must be frequently transported, mounted, dismounted, and loaded into cleaning stations. When these tasks are performed with inadequate auxiliary equipment, operators face elevated risks of disorders affecting the upper limbs, shoulders, neck, and lower back, which in turn contribute to high personnel turnover, production delays, and barriers to broader workforce inclusion. Compliance with occupational health standards, such as NOM-035-STPS-2018, further underscores the need for practical interventions that improve working conditions. This study applied the Design Thinking methodology to develop an ergonomic auxiliary device specifically intended for the transport and cleaning of injection molds. The process followed five sequential phases: empathizing with operators through observation and surveys, defining the core problem and design requirements, ideating and evaluating alternative concepts, prototyping the selected solution through CAD modeling and technical drawings, and evaluating the final design against the original requirements. Key requirements included mobility within the plant, adequate load capacity, reduced manual lifting, and compatibility with existing cleaning equipment. Iterative concept evaluation led to a compact design incorporating a bearing-and-shaft mechanism for raising and lowering the mold basket, constructed from structural steel (ASTM A36). Although budgetary constraints prevented the fabrication of a physical prototype, the CAD model and technical drawings were reviewed with supervisors and confirmed to meet the established ergonomic and operational criteria. The resulting auxiliary concept offers a user-centered solution expected to lower peak physical loads, decrease the likelihood of musculoskeletal disorders, shorten changeover-related times, and facilitate greater accessibility of machine-operator positions. The study demonstrates that Design Thinking can effectively translate operator needs into a technically documented industrial aid, providing a solid foundation for future physical prototyping, testing, and implementation in plastic injection environments

items.title: Artificial intelligence driven software systems for cardiovascular disease detection using physiological signals: a systematic review
items.abstract: Abstract Cardiovascular disease exacts an extraordinary global toll, with annual mortality exceeding 17.9 million lives and representing nearly one-third of all deaths worldwide. Reducing diagnostic delays, particularly in resource-limited settings, requires innovative, scalable, and cost-effective solutions. Artificial intelligence integrated with physiological signals, such as electrocardiogram (ECG), photoplethysmogram (PPG) and phonocardiogram (PCG), offers promising pathways for scalable, real-time cardiovascular assessment. Despite rapid advances, the evidence base remains fragmented, impeding identification of validated approaches and clinical translation pathways. A PRISMA-guided search across five databases (Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, Embase, IEEE Xplore) identified 35 eligible peer-reviewed studies. Quality and risk of bias were appraised using a QUADAS-2 adapted framework. Most systems utilised ECG (71.4%) with deep learning architectures, including convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Critical gaps were quantified: only 23% of studies conducted external validation, only 14% achieved clinical-scale deployment, no study integrated principled multi-signal fusion (ECG + PPG + PCG), and only one system (1/35, 2.9%) implemented a patient-facing conversational interface. Reported accuracies ranged from 70.5 to 99.9% (n = 21 reporting; unweighted mean 93.7%), but inconsistent metric reporting and limited external validation tempered translational confidence. A three-directional framework is proposed, addressing generalisability through multi-signal (ECG + PPG + PCG) models, interpretability through LLM-driven clinical narratives, and accessibility through edge-cloud deployment, to guide future research toward clinically deployable systems.

items.title: Assessment of Heavy Metal Concentrations in Educational Chalk and Associated Occupational Health Risks in Classrooms
items.abstract: Educational chalk can generate airborne dust during classroom activities, raising concerns about the presence of trace metals in products used regularly by teachers. This study examined the concentrations of selected metals in commercially available classroom chalk from Morogoro Municipality, Tanzania, and considered their potential occupational health implications. Five chalk brands—KCC Kemi, Fahari ya Morogoro, Continental, High Grade, and Okoa—were collected from local educational suppliers and schools. The samples were crushed, acid-digested, and analysed by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy. The elements investigated were lead (Pb), cadmium (Cd), chromium (Cr), zinc (Zn), and copper (Cu). Reported concentrations varied among the brands. Zinc concentrations ranged from 0.08 to 5.00 mg/kg, copper from 0.02 to 3.50 mg/kg, and chromium from 0.01 to 1.50 mg/kg. Lead was detected in KCC Kemi, Fahari ya Morogoro, and Continental chalk at concentrations of 0.80, 0.40, and 0.50 mg/kg, respectively, but was not detected in High Grade or Okoa chalk. KCC Kemi showed the highest reported concentrations of lead, chromium, zinc, and copper. These results indicate differences in the elemental composition of the selected chalk products. Because airborne metal exposure and health outcomes were not directly measured, the findings do not establish occupational risk levels. Further product monitoring and exposure assessment are warranted to inform the selection and use of classroom chalk.

items.title: Assessment of Occupational Health and Safety Knowledge among Butchers in the Cauvery Delta Region of Tamil Nadu, India
items.abstract: Retail butchers are exposed to occupational hazards associated with meat cutting, animal tissue handling, cleaning and other routine work activities. This study assessed knowledge of physical, biological, ergonomic, chemical and electrical hazards among 200 retail butchers in Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, Nagapattinam and Mayiladuthurai districts of Tamil Nadu, India. A cross-sectional survey was conducted during May–June 2026 using personal interviews and a structured, pre-tested questionnaire. Correct responses were expressed as frequencies and percentages, and mean percentage scores were calculated for each hazard domain. Knife cuts and lacerations were recognised by 83.0% of respondents, while 79.0% identified safe knife handling as a measure to prevent injuries. Awareness of biological hazards ranged from 63.0% for the safe handling of animal waste to 75.0% for risks associated with blood and body fluids. Knowledge was comparatively lower regarding awkward working postures (58.0%), chemical hazards (59.0%), repetitive cutting movements (60.0%) and electrical hazards (62.0%). The mean percentage scores were 73.4% for physical hazards, 68.8% for biological hazards, 63.6% for ergonomic hazards and 62.5% for both chemical and electrical hazards. The findings indicate variations in occupational-hazard knowledge, with notable gaps in ergonomic safety and the safe handling of chemicals and electrical equipment. Targeted occupational safety education addressing these gaps, biological risk prevention and appropriate protective measures is essential to improve occupational-hazard awareness among retail butchers.

items.title: ATLAS: Expert-Guided Sustainable Satellite Backhaul for Off-Grid Wildlife Monitoring
items.abstract: Remote wildlife monitoring increasingly depends on high-fidelity cameras and sensors deployed far from grid power and terrestrial networks. Low Earth orbit satellite links can provide connectivity in these settings, but their high power draw and variable bandwidth, combined with intermittent on-site solar harvesting, make continuous backhaul infeasible. Current systems therefore filter at the edge, with motion triggers that waste limited energy and bandwidth on environmental artifacts, or fixed vision models that cannot follow evolving expert objectives. We present ATLAS , an expert-guided edge-to-cloud system that treats satellite backhaul as a scarce resource for off-grid wildlife monitoring. ATLAS uses foundation models to compile natural-language expert intent into semantic scoring logic, combines semantic relevance with environmental and energy state, and uses a constrained reinforcement-learning scheduler to decide which clips to upload and when. As a representative case study, we deployed ATLAS for over six months across 18 off-grid salmon-monitoring river sites. ATLAS achieves a mean clip-selection accuracy of \(87.4\%\) , exceeding mean baseline accuracy by 26.4 percentage points, while maintaining near-continuous operation through low-solar periods in which baselines incur 16.0% downtime.

items.title: Auditable Authorization for LLM Agents: Empirical Evidence Across Model, Harness, and Workflow Layers
items.abstract: Human approval provides effective control only if rejected work stops and authorized work completes. We formalize refusal safety and bounded authorization completeness, and audit three execution boundaries: the model selects a call, the harness schedules and resumes it, and the workflow routes the decision to a protected effect. Paired decisions, exact traces, and native business-state witnesses support experiments with three models, five prompt arms, four runtime approval designs, two additional framework replays, and 100 public workflow sources. The paired model panel leaves seven of 300 approvals unfinished despite zero denied effects; parallel confirmation loses an approved branch in three tasks per model, restoration omits 336/672 CrewAI approvals, and four of 59 comparable n8n workflows execute after Reject. Comparing intent, generated calls, dispatch, and native effects identifies the first observable divergence and its repair target. This yields a practical audit contract that makes both refusal safety and authorization completeness independently verifiable, converting human approval from a procedural formality into an enforceable control boundary between intent and real-world effect.

items.title: Avaliação dos riscos ergonômicos e sua incidência na saúde dos trabalhadores da Agro Fundición, Santo Domingo, 2026
items.abstract: Introduction: This research aimed to evaluate ergonomic risks and musculoskeletal discomfort reported by workers at Agro Fundición, Santo Domingo, during 2026. Materials and Methods: A quantitative, descriptive, non-experimental, cross-sectional study was conducted, covering a census of 13 workers. Data collection involved a 15-question survey, direct observation, and the application of RULA and REBA assessment methods to three critical tasks. Frequencies, percentages, and cross-tabulations of REBA scores were analyzed. Results: Manual load handling was reported as frequent or constant by all 13 participants; prolonged standing, awkward postures, repetitive movements, and trunk rotation were each reported by 12 participants (92.3%). Similarly, 12 participants reported frequent or constant fatigue, as well as discomfort in the lower back, neck, shoulders, or arms. REBA scores were 12 for the casting process, 10 for polishing, and 5 for assembly; RULA scores were 7, 7, and 5, respectively. Discussion: A preventive plan was developed, incorporating engineering controls, work organization, training, and subsequent re-evaluation. Conclusions: The casting and polishing processes require priority attention. The findings characterize the level of exposure and perceived discomfort; the effectiveness of the proposed plan will require future evaluation.

items.title: B2G-Agent: An LLM-Based Multi-Agent Tool for End-to-End Building-Grid Interactions
items.abstract: Buildings are major electricity consumers and can interact with distribution network dispatch through flexible power scheduling. These interactions require distribution network operators (DNOs) and building energy managers (BEMs) to reconcile their operational constraints and perform complex cross-field computations. The lack of cross-domain expertise and unified computational workflows could lead to inefficient or physically infeasible interactions. To address this bottleneck, we develop an end-to-end large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent tool, B2G-Agent, that bridges DNOs and BEMs. The tool deploys three collaborative agents: a Translator for bidirectional cross-domain semantic mapping via hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); an Actor for automated configuration and execution of joint simulation and optimization through directed acyclic graphs; and a Reviewer for memory-augmented reflective failure diagnosis. This workflow abstracts away cross-field modeling complexities and enables both sides to focus on high-level operational decisions. Comprehensive evaluations across 200 synthesized tasks show that B2G-Agent improves the interaction quality score from 66.71 to 85.57 and increases the task success rate from 38.0% to 69.0% over the baseline while satisfying operational constraints. The open-source tool and interface are available at https://github.com/hkuedl/B2G-Agent.

items.title: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
items.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. Conventional graph backdoor attacks often lose effectiveness as models are updated across successive tasks, creating the impression that continual updates naturally weaken malicious associations. This work reveals a contrasting vulnerability: knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can also preserve early injected backdoors when the poisoned update is compatible with the clean-task signal being retained. For graph data, this risk is amplified by structural triggers, which are embedded into the message-passing paths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and can induce stable representation shifts across tasks. To expose this risk, we propose BadGCL, a model-agnostic framework for persistent backdoor attacks under a strict early-stage intervention setting. BadGCL learns topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective that couples poisoned gradients with clean-task optimization signals, together with a propagation consistency objective that stabilizes trigger-induced effects through graph message passing. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.

items.title: Behavioral Assurance for Socially Deployed AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.

items.title: Benchmarking the State of AI for Crop Yield Forecasting: A Global Assessment Across Modeling Paradigms
items.abstract: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for food security, agricultural policy, and commodity markets. Although statistical, process-based, and machine learning approaches have all been proposed, their relative strengths remain poorly understood due to the lack of large-scale, standardized comparisons. We address this gap through a comprehensive benchmark of five modeling paradigms -- statistical baselines, process-based models, conventional feature-engineered machine learning, deep sequence models, and tabular foundation models -- using the CY-Bench benchmark spanning 63 country-crop datasets (>12,000 administrative regions) across six continents. Beyond conventional pooled accuracy metrics, we introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that separately quantifies overall, spatial, temporal, and anomaly prediction skill. Across multiple crops and countries, feature-engineered machine learning and tabular foundation models achieve the strongest overall predictive performance. Data-driven models reduce NRMSE in 72% of countries growing maize and 78% of countries growing wheat, with median reductions of 8.8% and 11.9%, respectively. Across all modeling paradigms, spatial prediction is substantially easier than temporal and anomaly prediction. While data-driven models markedly improve temporal and anomaly prediction over statistical baselines, accurately forecasting year-to-year yield variability remains challenging. These findings suggest that future progress in large-scale crop yield forecasting will depend on the improved characterization of the environmental and management factors driving inter-annual yield variability, founded on effective representations for crop yield forecasting systems that support agricultural decision-making, early-warning applications, and food security planning
